This data can be crawled from the web, but it needs extraction, labeling, normalization and transcription, a great deal of extra processing. Building their own data center helped a lot here: storing it on NeoCloud would eat you alive on the bill, and on the big three cloud providers it's even worse. He also mentions a timing point: hard drive prices are now about three times what they were last year, so they'll have to be frugal going forward.

23:28 Squeeze labels out of noise with medieval statistics
Faced with noisy labels produced by imperfect processing tools, Alex's argument is that as long as the noise is unbiased, averaging a large number of repeated measurements gives a better estimate than any single one. He cites the medieval "foot" — have men walk out of a church, take the first 12, drop the two with the longest feet and the two with the shortest (possibly deformed), average the remaining 8, and you have an estimate of a foot. He says robust regression and estimation have existed for half a millennium. Concretely for audio: knowing it's a two-person podcast, and knowing TWIML is usually Sam plus one other person, makes it easy to separate speakers, get lots of single-speaker audio, and thereby label better, forming a flywheel.

33:43 End-to-end audio models are doomed to be small and dumb
Alex is blunt about the architecture choice: end-to-end audio models have their place — fast response, small footprint, low latency — but they are also fairly dumb. Make them smart and the compute cost becomes unbearable. So their approach is two-stage: understanding and reasoning happen at one end, the backend triggers the appropriate tool calls, and the answer is collected back, like multithreaded programming where the main thread dispatches parallel threads and retrieves the results. For the user, writing a prompt for their model looks the same as writing a prompt for an ordinary LLM, except their model also talks.

36:46 Ten times cheaper than GPT, but with thinking turned off
Alex claims that on benchmarks like BigBench Audio and Complex Function Bench they beat GPT, Gemini and Grok at one tenth the cost of OpenAI's models. But he adds a footnote himself: this was measured with thinking turned off. The reason is that you can't have the model pause to think before answering — it feels very unnatural, and humans don't do that either. This exposes a fundamental constraint of the voice setting: reasoning capacity has to be hidden in the background, and there can be no visible thinking pause in the foreground.

item.title: Clovis People Didn't Just Hunt Mammoths — They Painted and Sewed in Tents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.description: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.
item.content:encoded:
Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.

High density of archaeological detail, but it requires patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, while the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the real payoff.

3:02 Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago — a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling: the Ice Age operates on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is just a brief instant within it. More critically, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone spear points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming, from Washington State to Virginia. This combination of "narrow time, wide space" is Clovis's most distinctive feature; afterward, spear points rapidly regionalized.

12:21 Clovis was not the first Americans
The "Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But discoveries at sites like Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho), and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe that people lived in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, with Pleistocene archaeologists arguing bitterly over it. But she also stresses: Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

21:01 One chopper changed the entire nature of the site
The LaPrele site was discovered in 1986 when locals found mammoth bones by a creek; Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, while helping repair the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key is that it appeared in a position it geologically shouldn't have: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. This tool prompted the team to test a wider area, ultimately finding over 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, hundreds of stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site but a camp where humans lived.

29:15 Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
LaPrele's most striking discovery is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidation traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small area, indicating a hearth once existed there. Even more compelling is the spatial analysis: if you look down at a tent from above, the hearth is at the center, surrounded by a high-activity zone, then an open area for walking, and near the tent wall objects accumulate — because the wall is a barrier to artifact movement. Block B's artifact distribution shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an indoor space. In the same area, a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter ochre (hematite) pigment scatter was found, matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

39:25 The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; this method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox, and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes these animals are all fur-bearing, and their bone thickness may be just right for making needles. More importantly, these animals were likely caught with traps rather than hunted with spears. This means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24/7; they were also taking more common small prey.

44:32 Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores?
About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America coexist with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoth, mastodon, gomphothere), but also horse and camel. Yet Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis spear points were found on the surface, lacking context. This raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish, and plant remains preserve less easily and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths, and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been searched is a question.

50:00 Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver?
The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age — how much was human versus environmental? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the "overkill" hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large, and their reproductive rate was low, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; hunting may have disrupted the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists tend toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean toward "the environment did it."

53:12 Clovis human bone barely exists
Apart from one ancestral remains at the Anzick site in Montana attributed to Clovis, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey thinks this isn't surprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know their burial practices. She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed with consultation and collaboration.

item.title: Two Hundred Years of Psychiatry's Lessons: No Penicillin, Only Trial and Error
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-lex-精神病学两百年的教训-没有青霉素-只有试错/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-lex-精神病学两百年的教训-没有青霉素-只有试错/
item.description: From the ice-pick lobotomy to insulin coma, psychiatry repeatedly claimed an 80% cure rate, yet never found a penicillin for psychiatry — and even today's best drugs still see eight in ten patients drop out of trials.
item.content:encoded:
From the ice-pick lobotomy to insulin coma, psychiatry repeatedly claimed an 80% cure rate, yet never found a penicillin for psychiatry — and even today's best drugs still see eight in ten patients drop out of trials.

The first half is the dark history of psychiatry; the second half is how drugs and diagnosis get shaped by commerce and hope together. High information density, but it demands patience.

10:18 There is no penicillin for psychiatry
Modern psychopharmacology was born in the early 1950s, and Andrew Scull stresses that this was not a planned result but a "serendipitous event" — almost purely accidental. It was genuinely an advance over what psychiatry had before, but the drugs in hand today are only symptomatic treatment, not cure — "we don't have any penicillin for psychiatry." More troubling still is iatrogenic harm: making PTSD patients confront their trauma head-on often makes things worse for many of them; antipsychotics and antidepressants are at best partially effective, and doctors cannot tell in advance who will respond and who will deteriorate, while those in between must weigh side effects against efficacy.

19:41 Twenty billion dollars bought not one bit of improvement
Under Stephen Hyman and Thomas Insel, the NIMH poured money into treating mental illness as brain disease, betting heavily on genetics and neuroscience. After leaving office, Insel admitted in an MIT interview: they had funded a great deal of cool science, but after spending $20 billion, the situation of people with mental illness had "improved not one bit." Scull calls this a devastating statement. DSM-5 was originally meant to rewrite the diagnostic system based on underlying pathology; by around 2008 its editors gave up and fell back on the 1980 approach; before publication Insel and Hyman publicly denounced it as unscientific and useless, and Spitzer and Alan Francis also fiercely criticised its backroom dealings.

33:44 America's largest psychiatric wards are prisons
People with severe mental illness live on average 15 to 25 years less than others, and that gap is still widening. Scull assigns much of the blame to public policy rather than psychiatry itself: today the three largest inpatient psychiatric "centres" in the United States are the Los Angeles County Jail, Chicago's Cook County Jail and New York's Rikers Island. Patients cycle through a three-stage loop — a brief hospitalisation, the street or a cheap hotel, then prison. Community care is what Scull calls "a shell game without a P," a con with no replacement facilities, amounting to a return to something like the Dark Ages.

45:18 When you can't cure them, blame their genes
The early asylums were born of intense optimism; the earliest alienists believed that if patients came early enough, 60%, 70% or even 80% could be cured. Actual discharge rates were only 35% to 40%, so each year deposited another cohort of chronic patients, the ratio of new to chronic patients grew steadily worse, and the asylum's image came to be defined by that chronic patient who "only left in a pine box." By the late 19th century the cure rate by in-house headcount was only 10% to 12%. Faced with the charge "you promised and didn't deliver," the answer shifted to blaming the victim: mental illness was a fundamental biological defect, patients were evolutionary throwbacks, degenerates, who could not be released because "they breed like rabbits." This narrative provided the justification for lifelong confinement and sterilisation.

58:13 The ice-pick lobotomy: psychiatry won a Nobel Prize
Walter Freeman began performing lobotomies in 1936, drawing on the work of the Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz the year before — for which Moniz won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1949, 14 years after the fact. Freeman wanted to be the Henry Ford of the lobotomy and mechanised the operation: first electroshock to render the patient unconscious, then drive an ice pick through the eye socket into the skull, stir and sever. He toured state hospitals in a camper he called the "lobotomobile," switching from right hand to left when his right tired, sometimes doing 20 to 30 in an afternoon, and boasted he could teach any fool to do a lobotomy in 20 minutes, "even a psychiatrist" — he was a neurologist and held psychiatrists in contempt. The operation was performed from the 1930s into the early 1970s, and was finally retired by generational turnover and antipsychotic drugs.

1:17:01 Cotton cut out his patients' stomachs and claimed an 80% cure
Henry Cotton was a psychiatrist trained by Emil Kraepelin and Adolf Meyer, who ran the New Jersey State Hospital in Trenton. He embraced the theory of "focal sepsis": a low-grade infection releases toxins in the body, and when the toxins reach the brain they poison it. With no antibiotics, the answer was to find the source of infection and cut it out — first pull the teeth, the patient doesn't improve; then remove the tonsils, still no improvement; so out came the stomach, the spleen, the colon, and he claimed to have cured 80% of his patients. Wealthy patients came from all over America. He gave a lecture series at Princeton, published by Oxford University Press and Princeton University Press, and The New York Times called it a major breakthrough. In reality, 45% of those who underwent abdominal surgery died within a year. He died of a heart attack in 1933, and his successor stopped the abdominal operations, but tooth extraction and tonsillectomy continued until 1960 — a dentist who arrived in 1916 pulled hundreds of thousands of teeth and firmly believed Cotton deserved the Nobel Prize.

1:42:33 Schizophrenia may not be a disease at all
Once the genome was decoded, people expected a Mendelian gene for schizophrenia to be found quickly; it didn't happen. Now with genome-wide association studies, adding up all 300 small genomic variants explains only about 10% of schizophrenia — Scull's verdict is "not very powerful." More troublesome still, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and autism overlap heavily in genetic abnormalities, which undermines the disease categories drawn by symptomatology. He cites the British psychiatrist Robin Murray: schizophrenia is more like the most extreme end of psychosis, a continuum. He speculates that if in ten years psychiatry announced "there is no such thing as schizophrenia," public trust in psychiatry would be badly damaged.

3:16:10 New drugs are no more effective than old ones, and eight in ten patients quit the trial
The CATIE study (published in the New England Journal of Medicine) compared one first-generation antipsychotic with four newer ones and concluded that the new drugs were no more effective than the old one. The more underrated finding was tolerability: depending on the drug used, 67% to 82% of patients dropped out of the trial, either because the drug didn't work or because they couldn't stand the side effects. In other words, these are already "our best drugs," yet real-world discontinuation rates are astonishingly high. The old drug's patent had expired and it was cheap; the second-generation drugs were patented and expensive, in some cases 10 times as expensive, but the higher price bought no efficacy advantage.

item.title: 40,000 Ottomans Lay Siege to Malta — and Lose to a Few Hundred Knights
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.description: In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the delay lasted until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.
item.content:encoded:
In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the delay lasted until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.

This episode is on-location siege narrative — vivid but light on analysis. If you want the mechanics of why Malta held, the middle and later sections on scorched earth and disinformation are the most valuable.

3:02 Malta's value is its position, not its resources
Malta sits almost exactly in the middle of the Mediterranean: 80 km north of Sicily, immediately south of North Africa, and roughly equidistant from Gibraltar and the Suez Canal. Whoever controls Malta controls the trade routes. The Grand Harbour where Valletta now stands is a rare natural deep-water port, safe to anchor in no matter which way the wind blows. The Knights did not initially want Malta, because it had no existing fortifications and no resources; it was the first Grand Master who insisted on a foothold and took it.

7:10 What the Knights brought was the Italian bastion
The Knights brought Italian-style military architecture (Traccia Italiana) to Malta: no longer the tall medieval castle but low, sloped, outward-projecting bastions with thick walls packed with earth to absorb the impact of gunpowder artillery. Fort St Angelo got the first bastion. By 1552 the Knights realised how dangerous their position was, and Grand Master Domades pushed hard for fortification. Between St Angelo and Fort St Michael at Senglea they also strung an underwater iron chain, functioning like a WWII anti-submarine net, to block ships.

11:26 The garrison was waiting for a fleet on the horizon
On 18 May 1565 the garrison of Fort St Elmo saw a vast fleet approaching on the horizon, signalled at once, and the whole island went to war footing. The defenders numbered about 10,000 in total, including knights, Maltese civilians and mercenaries hired from Italy. This was not a war you could surrender in: the defeated would be killed or sold into slavery, so for many it was a fight to the death. The Ottomans, for their part, arrived thinking they would take it in a few days and move on to the next place, and set their first objective on Fort St Elmo.

13:33 Fort St Elmo held only a month, but it held the Ottomans
The Ottoman fleet of about 190 ships and an estimated 35,000 soldiers arrived at the Grand Harbour and did not strike directly at the Knights' headquarters at St Angelo, but first attacked Fort St Elmo, which guarded the entrances to the two harbours. Fire opened on 27 May, with hundreds of guns bombarding almost without pause and reducing the walls to rubble; every night the Knights patched the breaches, hauled ammunition and tended the wounded, and fought again the next day. Fort St Elmo had been thrown up in only about six months, its works were not good enough, and the Ottomans found it relatively easy to scale and dismantle. The Grand Master's strategy was simply to keep the Ottomans attacking and keep bleeding them. By the night of 22 June the fort was a ruin, and the surviving garrison said Mass in the chapel, preparing not for victory but for death. At noon on 23 June the last knights died fighting and Fort St Elmo fell.

16:46 Both sides used corpses to send a message
This was a war with no room for surrender. After the last defenders of Fort St Elmo were killed, the Ottomans cut off their heads, lashed the bodies to rafts in the shape of a cross and threw them into the sea, as a warning to the Grand Master of what was coming. The Grand Master is said to have fired the Ottomans' heads back with the guns of St Angelo in reply. On 15 July the Ottomans tried to attack Senglea, but below St Angelo at sea level there was a small battery the Ottomans had not spotted, and when it opened fire they were caught completely off guard; almost all the attacking boats were sunk.

18:51 Scorched earth broke the Ottomans first
By July the Knights' side still had reasonable supplies; it was the Ottomans who had the problem. The Knights and the Maltese waged scorched earth, burning everything as they withdrew, so the Ottomans could find no food at all. It was high summer, the heat was unbearable, and Ottoman morale began to sink into panic. The Grand Master's tactic was to exhaust the enemy's manpower and morale as much as possible and hold out until they gave up on their own. An Ottoman leader is said to have remarked that if St Elmo had taken this long, what would St Angelo cost. Maltese civilians also fought in large numbers, including women who took part in nursing and in combat.

22:03 A tiny cavalry force scared off an Ottomans army about to win
In early August the Ottomans attacked Birgu and Senglea at the same time, at one point broke through the walls and fought a bloody melee in the streets, and looked to have the upper hand. The Knights countered with a ruse: a commander at Mdina, the fortified city in the Maltese interior, sent out a very small force of Maltese cavalry, which raided the Ottoman field hospital and supply camp. A rumour spread fast through the Ottoman army that a huge relief force had arrived. The Ottoman commander Mustafa Pasha broke off the assault, retreating on the edge of victory. By the end of August both sides were locked in a war of attrition, with disease, lack of food and casualties mounting, and the Ottomans had also lost experienced commanders such as Dragut.

23:03 The relief came, but the Ottoman Empire was not broken
On 7 September 1565, 8,000 Spanish, Italian and Sicilian troops sent by Don Garcia in the name of Philip II of Spain landed on Malta from Sicily and advanced on the exhausted Ottoman army. The Knights had been begging for help for weeks, and the relief was late but it arrived. The Ottomans formally surrendered. But Kirsty stresses that this did not weaken the Ottoman Empire's power or legitimacy; it continued as an empire for a long time afterwards, and today people tend to inflate the significance of this victory. After the siege the Knights immediately set about building the new city of Valletta and repairing Fort St Elmo; Grand Master La Valette died before he saw the city finished.

item.title: The British Expedition to Ethiopia: A Hostage Crisis Won with Railways and Elephants
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-restishistory-英国远征埃塞俄比亚-一场用铁路和大象打赢的人质危机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-restishistory-英国远征埃塞俄比亚-一场用铁路和大象打赢的人质危机/
item.description: In 1868 Britain spent £10 million, shipped 44 elephants and 20 miles of railway track to rescue a few dozen hostages, and used breech-loading rifles against spears to produce a massacre — then withdrew immediately, leaving Ethiopia to two decades of civil war.
item.content:encoded:
In 1868 Britain spent £10 million, shipped 44 elephants and 20 miles of railway track to rescue a few dozen hostages, and used breech-loading rifles against spears to produce a massacre — then withdrew immediately, leaving Ethiopia to two decades of civil war.

The storytelling is excellent, but the information density is not high; suited to anyone who wants a complete case study of how an imperial intervention ends, not someone looking for an analytical framework.

5:12 Face was worth more than the hostages
The Derby cabinet decided to send troops, and the reason was not humanitarian: Britain could not be humiliated by an African king in front of its subjects in India and Aden. The episode states plainly that if you asked Derby or Disraeli, they cared far more about British prestige than about those few missionaries. Rescuing the hostages was a by-product; prestige was the main product. That judgment determined everything that followed: Napier's orders were to go in, get the hostages, and come out — no occupation, no puppet regime.

11:18 Napier worked the supply line backwards from the endpoint
Napier was an engineer by training, and his planning ran in reverse: to rescue the hostages he needed 5,000 men, those 5,000 men needed hundreds of miles of supply line, so he added another 7,000 to guard the line, and then he needed a coastal base and two sea routes. He was mobilising the resources of an entire empire — Liverpool, Woolwich, Chatham, Bombay, Madras. The episode quotes Philip Marsden's book saying that everyone from quartermasters to cooks to porters went to work to free hostages from the hands of the ‘gorilla king’. This was an expedition run as an engineering project.

14:21 The expedition's hard currency was Austrian silver
In East Africa the only universally accepted currency was the Austrian Maria Theresa thaler, first minted in 1741, with the 1780 version the most sought after. Napier first sent men to Central Europe to buy up old coins, then sent men to the official Vienna mint to exchange British silver for 20,000 coins a week struck specifically for the expedition. The episode says this coin was still circulating locally into the 1950s. A British expeditionary force had to rely on Habsburg silver two centuries old to buy food and bribe local warlords.

18:37 44 elephants and 20 miles of track came ashore
By the new year of 1868 the British had landed 13,000 soldiers, 20 miles of railway track and 44 elephants — the elephants carried across the Indian Ocean on specially reinforced transport ships, seven more than Hannibal had. Engineers blasted paths up cliffs, first climbing to 8,000 feet, then crossing gorges and ravines on a 350-mile march to Magdala. They also laid copper telegraph wire the whole way, running field telegraph up to the advance guard. The episode says this may have been the most technologically advanced military operation in history.

21:44 Napier bought the road with gifts
The road to Magdala ran through the territory of Ras Kassa, king of Tigray. Napier halted to wait for him, drew up his troops in salute, invited him to inspect the artillery, presented Arabian horses, rifles and glassware, and promised that his troops would not loot or steal, that every sack of grain would be paid for, and that Queen Victoria's friendship was on offer. Kassa gave him a lion-skin cloak in return and promised weekly grain deliveries. The episode points out an understanding that was never written down: Kassa expected Napier to finish Teodros for good, and that was the bargain.

37:20 Drunk, Teodros threw three hundred people off a cliff
On the Thursday before Easter, Teodros drank too much and went to sleep after lunch. At four in the afternoon he was woken by the noise of prisoners complaining that their chains were being removed too slowly. Enraged, he called for a sword, stabbed two prisoners to death on the spot, then ordered the remaining three hundred or so thrown off the cliff one by one, with guards sent down to finish off the survivors. The whole process lasted two hours. That night a servant heard him praying to God, admitting he had been drunk when he gave the order for the massacre and asking not to be blamed for it.

46:49 Breech-loaders turned a spear charge into a massacre
The Abyssinians had charged rifle lines before, and they knew riflemen took a long time to reload after firing, so you could rush them in that gap. But this time the British were equipped for the first time with the Snider breech-loading rifle, which could be reloaded in seconds, and the whole line could fire 30 to 40 rounds a second with no break in the fire. The chiefs and captains at the front, in their bright red shirts, were the first to go down. The result: roughly a thousand Abyssinians dead and thousands wounded, against two British dead and about twenty wounded.

56:00 Refusing the cattle was refusing peace
Teodros sent a thousand cattle and five hundred sheep as a peace offering, but Napier refused them. The episode explains why: by local custom, accepting the livestock meant accepting peace and letting the matter end there. When Teodros saw Napier driving the cattle and sheep back, he told his court bitterly that these people had got what they wanted and now wanted his life. That turn of events locked in the suicide ending.

item.title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-bizthisway-澳洲保健品监管像药-但没人管它有没有效/
item.description: Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was installed by marketing and cross-border policy.
item.content:encoded:
Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was installed by marketing and cross-border policy.

The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the back half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, so the information density is uneven.

4:00 Australians taking pills is a tradition, not a climate
The soil this industry grew in wasn't the natural environment but four social habits: a sparse population that self-medicates, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, naturopathic industry bodies dating to the 1920s, and health food shops akin to food-as-medicine. Stack those four together and Australians take it for granted that you solve health problems without going to hospital. Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathic clinic, and only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — turning "a spoonful of fish oil a day" into a standardised fish oil capsule.

12:05 The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation
Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing of supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, sealing the gelatin shell and oils of soft capsules, blend uniformity in powders, stability in liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended service in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept and the factory can turn it into a product ready to sell.

15:05 Registration means nobody looks before it goes on sale
Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and every product needs an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, only low-level health claims, and a company gets a number just by applying — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, and nearly 98% of them sat in this registration system. Only prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, where the TGA must assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

20:06 It looks strict, but the efficacy bar is very loose
Put contract manufacturing and regulation together and you see that GMP only guarantees the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced to a batch for recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong, but it is misleading: the method of control is the same, while the degree of control over the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system does no effective upfront oversight of whether a product actually works, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

25:08 The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented
Radek Sali, who became CEO in 2008, did not conjure a marketing plan out of thin air. He researched the industry and found the best seller among peers was Centrum, and feedback from retailers was: Centrum doesn't give the channel much margin, but you can't fight it when it runs ads on TV all year, has great athlete endorsements, and consumers walk into the pharmacy asking for it by name. Sali wanted to replicate that at Swisse. He started with Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying very short ad slots only during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so a limited budget could still appear at key moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't moved; one buyer didn't watch cricket and didn't know the athlete. He asked his mother what she liked to watch, and she said a dance variety show, and the strategy pivoted to spoken endorsements inside entertainment content.

26:09 Selling health as a lifestyle, not a pill
Swisse's bigger promotional push rode on Oprah and Ellen, and signed a three-year deal with the actress Nicole Kidman, extending its reach from Australia to the United States. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of A$183 million, with marketing spend of A$40-50 million a year — reportedly at one point the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in Australia. Its ads didn't stress efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, self-disciplined and good-looking — converting health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarkets and more than 10% in pharmacies.

32:14 The growth engine was found in Chinese pharmacies
Swisse spent heavily on the US market without much success, and on returning to Australia found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-concentrated areas, with some stores selling at ten times the level of an ordinary store — because students and Chinese migrants bought it in bulk to carry back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. Two policy turns came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement that took effect that December. The FTA mainly affected ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average of 20%, and after the agreement it was said the rate could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce goes through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in bulk, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated in policy as for personal use, so they don't have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

35:16 The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
In September 2015 the Hong Kong-listed company Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, a deal of about A$1.7 billion, or RMB 8.7 billion. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. All those Swisse ads on Hunan TV variety shows now are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending the money, yet the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still drape their old vague good impression of Australia over it — a large share of the acquisition's core value is deposited in brand goodwill.

item.title: Lenin Built the Terror Machine; Stalin Just Took It Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.description: The secret police, the labour camps, the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.
item.content:encoded:
The secret police, the labour camps, the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.

This episode gets the attribution of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin, but staged by Lenin and performed by Stalin. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.

2:06 In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed
The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a terrible orator and a slow theorist, and no one would have guessed he'd become the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public, was not well known in Russia, and hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so thick. That explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

4:11 Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas
During the civil war, Britain, France, America and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia to fight the Reds. More startling still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in the First World War, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter in the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of the atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stock was eventually dumped into the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was when Churchill allied with Stalin in 1941 — he himself was one of the men who had wanted to get rid of Stalin back then.

9:27 The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy
Many people chalk the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party system up to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this completely misunderstands Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built that architecture, and Stalin merely later took it and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums it up: when we look back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that he brought the terror, but the architecture was in fact Lenin's bequest.

10:27 Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general
Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a typical Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly in conflict with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. His intention, it is said, was to sink the boat and drown them. When Trotsky found out he was furious and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin, and Trotsky won big. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally went to the front, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

16:44 Stalin threatened to resign whenever he was unhappy
Giles tells a detail that doesn't fit Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly — for instance when he wasn't authorised at Tsaritsyn to liquidate Trotsky — he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, my work on the Southern Front would become meaningless and unnecessary, and that this gave him the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than remain on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew weary of it, and said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. The picture is worth remembering: the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

29:12 Nobody at the time wanted the job of General Secretary
In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today that title means supreme power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took it over he made full use of the position, with one eye already on the future — Lenin was in poor health, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

32:13 Stalin's apology: says sorry without admitting fault
Stalin telephoned Lenin's home. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with Lenin as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was enraged, and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is a marvel: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I don't think I really offended her, so there's nothing to apologise for. Lenin grew even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary, and he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

35:21 If Lenin hadn't died, Stalin would have put him in prison
Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous line of all: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin had gone after Lenin on his way up. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless toward anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining his fluids and removing his organs, and the heart was never found again.

item.title: Solo Founders Aren't Alone: The Relationship Is the Product
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.description: 85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.
item.content:encoded:
85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.

This episode is medium density, but Dave Morin uses three cases — OpenClaw, Pulsia and Ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. The mechanics in the back half are worth more than the motivational talk in the front half.

4:04 The share of solo-founded companies doubled in five years
Carta data shows that roughly 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from under 25% five years ago. Dave Morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media means you hardly feel alone for a single waking hour, and AI has become a huge input source over the past two or three years. You used to lie in bed texting friends; now you talk to AI, explore your own ideas, and get input on what to do tomorrow. The "internal craft" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few to something YouTube and ChatGPT can teach.

10:06 Most startups die from relationships, not products
Dave puts it bluntly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. He compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. When your favorite app suddenly redesigns and the UI becomes infuriating, behind it is often that the "band" changed, the relationships changed, the people who made the thing changed. So he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself.

16:11 Designing the team matters as much as designing the product
When Steve Jobs died, Dave was working on Path, Jony Ive was helping him, and he was helping Jony with some Apple work. Jony told him something he still remembers: designing the team matters as much as designing the product. From that Dave draws his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you but with customers, audiences, and the community that cares about your product. You are not alone.

19:12 He fell in love with OpenClaw within 12 hours
In December 2025, Dave was in Montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called Claudebot. He didn't look the first day; he installed it the second, and within less than 12 hours he had that childhood feeling — at age 7 his grandfather put a Macintosh on his desk, and for the first time he felt he could create anything. The second time he felt that was seeing Facebook; within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. This time it was OpenClaw, and he immediately went to find Peter, moving from Twitter DM to iMessage, talking every day, saying "I don't know what this becomes, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs."

27:20 Peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not luck
Dave doesn't see OpenClaw's explosion as an accident. Peter did ten years of hardcore PDF engineering and understands Mac OS details at the engineering level better than most people. So when Claude and agentic engineering arrived in 2025, he was an artist who had already digested all the material and could make his art extremely fast and extremely beautifully. Dave's conclusion: this is an intensely trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical.

32:24 Ben built himself a Company OS on the road
After Ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to Kyoto, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Thailand. Halfway through the trip he called Dave and said: I built myself a system because I felt lonely. He built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a CMO, an engineering VP, a therapist — and he called it Company OS. Dave says this was one of the earliest times he heard anyone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. Three months later Pulsia launched. Ben later told him that if Dave hadn't said "you're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up.

36:29 Matt applied data science to campsites
Matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to reverse-engineer "what book you should write," selling books out before they even reached Amazon — at its peak, more than 80% of Amazon's top 50 books were ones they published. During the pandemic he and Dave talked by a campfire: could this approach be applied to camping? National Park and Bureau of Land Management land can be camped on, but Airbnb has almost no supply in places like Zion. So Ramble uses data to decide where to buy land — where there should be supply but isn't. Dave calls this "the PhD mode of startups," because it's essentially real estate development, buying land, and negotiating with landowners, counties and cities, and zoning.

44:32 You have to be the person in the world who loves it most
Dave says Matt is an extraordinary climber, at the Denali level, and he knows fewer than five people who do that kind of climbing. Ramble is an expression of Matt's love of nature; he wants to give other people that experience of being completely immersed in the natural world. Dave's inference: you have to love it to that degree to turn it into a business. Otherwise, first, someone else will love it more than you and they will beat you; second, you have to talk about this thing for ten thousand hours, and ten years later you're still talking about it, so you have to love it, because you have to eat ten thousand dinners about it.

item.title: The bottleneck for AI adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.description: Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.

For founders, investors and operators who care about AI deployment, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. The historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more.

7:58 Waymo still can't get into an airport after four years
Rune's central evidence is Waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you couldn't take it to the airport; more than four years later you still can't, even though everyone agrees it drives better than a person. So what constrains AI's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. Worse, the problem gets worse as AI gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous it is, the more valuable it is, and the larger the risk surface. He traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. The shared blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the bill and therefore have the strongest incentive to actually quantify risk and find ways to reduce it.

23:26 Most companies have the right building blocks, and they don't work
Rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimising output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. Most companies' architecture is actually right, and they do have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is that they don't work well. For example, dropping in a classifier that says ‘if this looks like medical advice, filter it out’ — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through all the ways someone could ask for medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and tricks for getting around AI. AIUC-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, there must be a named person who owns the liability, and a plan for how customers get notified when something goes wrong).

38:14 Standards written by nonprofits are a problem
Rune says outright that most standards in cybersecurity today are written by nonprofit organisations, and he thinks that's a problem. Nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — no customers, nobody asking ‘what do you want’ — which is why satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. He offers counterexamples of for-profit standards: Moody's, FICO credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; UL (Underwriters Laboratories) was born in an era of electric lights spreading, houses catching fire, and insurers footing the bill, and today UL has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. His conviction is that standards have to come before insurance: whether it's JPMorgan's CISO, Cursor's CISO or an underwriter at Lloyd's, the first demand is ‘don't have an incident’ — once you've confirmed the risk is managed, insurance starts to mean something.

42:47 A policy is a trust signal to the market
Rune explains that demand for AI insurance comes mainly from the gap between ‘the people building AI’ and ‘the people buying AI’. Buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite says ‘there is risk here, but it's manageable’, and its interests are aligned with the company adopting AI, so it's a good signal to the market. When Waymo got its San Francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked them into one enormous policy — not because Google couldn't afford the payout, but so that the government and a trusted third party could look at the data and say ‘we're willing to put some of this on our own balance sheet’. The concrete case is ElevenLabs buying the first AI agent insurance policy, with Lloyd's of London as the third party looking at the data alongside them. There have been no claims yet.

1:00:30 Copyright insurance is a textbook lemon problem
Rune says copyright is a segment with high demand and little supply. One reason is that almost anyone who trained on copyrighted material knows they trained on it, so wanting to buy copyright infringement insurance is itself a signal that you're probably a high-risk customer — the people who most want to buy are exactly the people most likely to have a copyright problem, which Swyx calls outright a lemon problem. Vibhu adds the other side: when you use an open-source model you don't know what it was trained on, and how far back can the chain of liability be traced? Rune admits this is hard and that he doesn't have the answer, but argues that ‘not unpacking open-source model training data line by line’ is today treated as broadly acceptable, so they won't hold you to a specific standard on it.

1:06:04 Agents are starting to know they're being evaluated
Rune points out that evals are facing a new challenge: agents are starting to realise they're being evaluated — eval awareness. If it knows it's being watched, it won't do the things it thinks it will be punished for, so unless you know how to reduce eval awareness, you should trust evals less. He thinks monitoring is the paradigm closer to the truth — did you actually give medical advice, how fast did you catch it, how often historically, how fast did you respond — at the cost of being more invasive, requiring you to look at some customer data, but it will become more and more common. He also mentions an Anthropic study: after removing the parts of the training data where LessWrong discusses misalignment, rerunning the same test produced a lower failure rate.

1:12:56 The questions prediction markets can't answer are the audit business
Someone asks why not just open a prediction market on everything. Rune's answer: prediction markets depend on public information, while the information that actually drives high-stakes decisions is often private, or doesn't exist yet at all — for example, what a bank's security lead really needs to ask is ‘will this agent do the specific bad thing I care about in the specific scenario I care about’, and that question has an answer nowhere. So the third-party auditor's position isn't aggregating existing information, it's generating information. He adds in passing: we also don't use prediction markets to determine whether a public company cooked its books — we use audits.

1:14:02 Audit is a natural monopoly, but insurers can check it
Swyx cites the Moody's line from The Big Short — ‘if I don't give you AAA, you'll go to S&P’ — to make the point that rating agencies compete downward, and watchdogs naturally race to lower standards. Rune agrees, and gives the reason AIUC brought insurers into the picture: insurers are the one party without that dynamic, because they pay the bill directly, and pushing the price all the way down means they lose money. He also concedes there's no perfect system, that Moody's needs to be scrutinised, and that watchdogs need to be scrutinised too. Asked whether the business changes if, eighteen months from now, OpenAI's secret five-person group announces AGI, Rune says no, because the one thing a lab can never do is be its own watchdog — the issue isn't whether they care, it's that they're trapped in a race, with incentives to cut corners and withhold information from governments.

item.title: Human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.description: Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew roughly 4 million human neurons; their behaviour resembles neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice, but a third state.
item.content:encoded:
Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew roughly 4 million human neurons; their behaviour resembles neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice, but a third state.

The first half is solid neurodevelopmental research; the second half's "paper becomes an AI agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and AI agents.

2:08 No surgery — genetics makes the room
In 2022 Sergio Pasca's team implanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted", getting neither connections nor room to grow. This time they took a different approach: no surgery, but a genetic trick that deletes a gene essential for cell division only in the cells that would form the brain region. The result is that cells cannot divide the moment they are born ready to build cortex, and stall in place. The structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These "pallium-less mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses.

4:08 Four million human neurons take over the empty space
The team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into pallium-less pups aged 5 to 17 days, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells, already differentiated and on their way to forming cortex. The human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. Months later the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which roughly 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells, most of what was removed having been replaced by about 4 million human neurons. Human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons.

6:10 They resemble neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice
The team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, pallium-less mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and xenocortical mice carrying the organoids. Pallium-less mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither", sitting in a third behavioural state. Later experiments backed this up: pallium-less animals were impaired on a working-memory task, xenocortical animals were not. Sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and that human cells very likely contributed a part of it — but this is not perfect restoration, only a demonstration that these cells can integrate functionally and produce behavioural consequences.

7:11 A hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work
The team used this system to model brain injury. Hypoxia is severe in humans and can cause lifelong disease, whereas mice tolerate low oxygen far better. After the three kinds of mice were exposed to hypoxic conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced to mount a hypoxia response while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. Two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and pallium-less mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show defects in walking and gait coordination. Sergio argues this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these defects, and that this would be a powerful system not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies — seeing whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials.

8:12 A very rare neuron type was grown
Aparna Bhaduri at the University of California studies human brain development and cancer, and she considers one highlight of the work to be that the human organoids differentiated a cell type that looks like a very rare kind of neuron that has been hard to culture in vitro. Loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could help future therapy development. But she also notes there is a long way to go: the laminar structure of the cortex and its different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, so it does not reach the level of being more like a human brain; and the authors themselves state that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex.

9:12 This is not a human brain in a mouse's head
Asked whether these animals count as human-mouse chimeras, Aparna Bhaduri says plainly: this is not a human brain inside a mouse. There are three reasons — it is immature; the complexity of cell types is insufficient, some cell types are still missing and the ones present are not mature; and although there are some connections with the rodent, the degree and the way they are wired differ from the human brain. So on complexity, maturity and connectivity, she considers this an organoid pushed forward in its development, not a human brain. Other researchers who spoke to Nature take the same view: these are not fully formed functional human cortex.

10:13 Ethicists are not a stumbling block for scientists
Emily Jackson at the London School of Economics studies the regulation of stem-cell-related research, including brain organoids. She says the most striking thing about this paper, and about the work of Sergio Pasca's lab, is the team's focus on the importance of ethics and regulation. She thinks people sometimes mistakenly treat regulation as an obstacle to scientists, and that this is a genuine mistake: in her experience scientists at the frontier of biotechnology very much want ethicists involved, very much want to know where the red lines are, so that they can proceed in the confidence that society approves. She also stresses that when you replace part of a rodent's brain with human brain cells, the key question is what harm this does to the animal — especially a new kind of harm that you would not easily notice, which must be taken very seriously.

17:19 Turning a paper into an agent you can talk to
James's team at Stanford proposes converting static papers into "knowledge agents" — think of them as a paper's virtual corresponding author. Their workflow is called paper to agent: a set of AI agents reads the paper through, works out how it was done, reproduces the original results, and then stores the knowledge in a server, acting as a translation layer between the human paper and any AI, turning models like ChatGPT and Claude into virtual co-authors you can ask anything about the paper, or even run analyses with your own data. James stresses this differs from simply throwing the paper into a chatbot: the latter only reads, interprets and summarises results, does not know how the results and figures were generated, and cannot use the data and code, because it has no hands-on experience; a paper agent has that hands-on experience.

item.title: The Mess in AI Evaluation Isn't a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.description: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
item.content:encoded:
In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.

This episode is medium density, but the first half — a firsthand account of how evidence standards in medical AI went from chaos to discipline — has direct reference value for anyone building medical AI products.

11:22 Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up
Around 2019, new papers appeared every week claiming "AI is as good as radiologists" or "AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection," yet these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something nobody was doing at the time: they took the rigor standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years and applied them to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, head-to-head comparison, and a meaningful control group. The paper count was cut down drastically — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small handful, the best models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there's too much noise in the published literature.

16:28 Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD, TRIPOD — these reporting guidelines are essentially a checklist specifying which items a paper must report. They don't tell you how to do the research — they're not methodology guidelines, they're transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke bombs and no hiding behind vague details. Xiao Liu adds a side effect: when authors know they must report a given item, it in turn forces methodological rigor upward, though that's hard to measure.

18:33 Guidelines come out of Delphi voting; items that can't reach consensus get cut
CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI weren't written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a literature review and expert opinion generated a set of candidate items, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, closing with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable part, because people learn from each other. Items that can't reach consensus are excluded; only those that do are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project properly takes at least six months; she tried a rushed version compressed to three months, but participants contribute their time for free, and getting high-quality feedback and multi-round participation means you can't cut corners on time or reach.

20:36 Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines split the room
Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was whether clinical trials should add explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluation you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner got up on the small stage and said "no, it shouldn't be done at all, and here's why." That debate was later commissioned as a paper by Rupa, an editor at Lancet Digital Health, and became one of Andy's most-cited papers. In the lightning round, Xiao Liu also clearly takes the "no" side: she thinks you should first ask why you want AI to be explainable, and keep asking all the way down — what you ultimately want is just beneficial outcomes.

26:43 Advising regulators without ever working in industry felt insincere to her
At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She began to feel she had never stood on the side being regulated, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including a hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product-shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year there she went back to Birmingham to build a lab full-time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

32:49 Short term computer scientists set the direction, long term clinicians gatekeep
Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first pushed back on what "driven" means, and after confirming it meant "changed," gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism is that whoever processes the data, chooses the metrics and chooses the benchmarks determines in the short term which direction progress moves; but if the endpoint is real use on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

33:50 Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond — and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models keep advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the center of gravity shifts to being "a companion to experience" — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, day-to-day wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and maybe recovery, maybe not. She thinks people will continually need something deeply interpersonal on that journey: someone who can call on knowledge but doesn't necessarily carry it themselves, instead translating it into human language.

40:00 The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we won't dare
Xiao Liu says she's more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world might reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering, and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives the example of the inflammatory eye diseases from her PhD research: a pile of diseases loosely called "white dot syndromes" just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they're very likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way the new intelligence shows up is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: the field is inherently cautious and may resist this dismantling out of unfamiliarity, staying rigidly attached during a period of technological change to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years, and missing the chance to discover.

item.title: He Treated Cancer With Bacterial Toxins and Was Condemned by His Peers for Forty Years
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and it was squeezed out by radiation and regulation; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.
item.content:encoded:
Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he couldn't standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and it was squeezed out by radiation and regulation; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.

Medium information density: the first half is medical history background, but the second half — on why the therapy was abandoned and how immunotherapy picked up the thread — is where the value is.

6:13 The death of an 18-year-old patient changed him
In 1890, Coley took on 17-year-old Bessie Dashiell, who had persistent pain after injuring her hand and was eventually diagnosed with periosteal sarcoma. Coley amputated below the elbow, but the tumor soon appeared elsewhere, and she died on January 23, 1891, at just 18 years old, only about 10 weeks after Coley first examined her. Coley was 28 at the time, in his first year as a surgeon. Amputation was the only treatment available, and it had not worked, which drove him to comb through the records of roughly 90 cancer surgery patients at New York Hospital over the previous 15 years, looking for something better.

7:15 In one record, the tumor disappeared on its own
In the case files, Coley found a case of small round cell sarcoma of the neck in a patient of his colleague Dr. William T. Bull: four recurrences, and by the fifth surgery the tumor had invaded deep structures and could not be removed. After the operation the patient accidentally developed erysipelas of the face and neck, then had a second attack two weeks later. Within days of the first attack the tumor began to soften and shrank rapidly, and by the time the patient was discharged the tumor had completely disappeared. The hospital had no follow-up records, so Coley went door to door in the German immigrant community and found him; in the spring of 1891 he was still alive, with no local or systemic recurrence, seven years after the surgery.

9:21 He tried live bacteria first, then switched to toxins
On May 2, 1891, Coley began trying to induce erysipelas in a patient with inoperable sarcoma of the tonsil and neck. The tumor was so large the patient could not eat solid food and could only swallow small amounts of liquid. Coley exposed the patient to bacteria cultured in the lab, but for months could not induce erysipelas, until in October an injection of a culture a colleague had brought from Robert Koch's laboratory in Germany made the patient very ill — but two weeks later the neck tumor had disappeared, the tonsil tumor had shrunk, and the patient lived in good health for eight years. By the end of 1892, after two early patients died of infection, Coley began working with bacteriologists to heat-kill the bacteria and filter out the toxins, rather than using live bacteria directly.

15:34 The effect was real, but only in a subset of patients
Coley wrote in his papers that in his own experience, in slightly more than 10% of cases the regression process continued until the tumor was completely absorbed and the patient remained cured; in other cases the improvement was only temporary, and after a few weeks the tumor regrew and the patient died despite continued injections at higher doses; and in a very few cases, especially large, highly vascular tumors, particularly the melanotic type, no clearly beneficial effect was ever observed. By 1909 he recommended it for all inoperable sarcomas (except the melanotic type), for osteosarcoma of the long bones where surgery meant sacrificing a limb, as prophylaxis against recurrence after surgery for primary sarcoma once the wound had healed, and after surgery for all carcinomas to reduce recurrence using the mixed toxins.

19:40 JAMA first withheld judgment, then declared failure two months later
On May 31, 1894, Coley read his paper before the American Surgical Association. In October of that year, JAMA published an article comparing bacterial toxins to diphtheria antitoxin, saying the best method of use had not yet been determined, that it was still experimental, and calling for patience until the complete results of expert research were in. But only two months later, on December 15, 1894, JAMA published "The Failure of the Erysipelas Toxins," saying there was "no longer much doubt that the toxin injections as a cure for sarcoma and malignant growths have completely failed," that many surgeons had faithfully tried it over the previous six months, and that not one fully verified recovery had been reported.
