Coley responded the following January, pointing out that he had used not only erysipelas toxins but also Bacillus prodigiosus, and saying that the failure of a few doctors in a limited number of cases would not affect the scientific community's judgment of whether the method succeeded or failed.

23:47 Forty years, a thousand patients, a hundred and fifty papers
Coley worked with these toxins for about 40 years, treated roughly 1,000 cancer patients, and published about 150 papers. In 1909 he wrote that 52 cases of inoperable sarcoma had been successfully treated with a mixed toxin of erysipelas and Bacillus prodigiosus, of which 35 remained healthy for 3.25 to 16 years, 28 for 5 to 16 years, and 14 for 10 to 16 years. Although Park, Davis, and Company produced various preparations starting in 1899, the toxins never became the most common treatment for inoperable sarcoma. The reasons included: tense relations with his boss James Ewing, who opposed his research; the bone sarcoma registry refusing to include his cured patients, insisting they had been misdiagnosed; his insistence that all cancers had a microbial origin, even after that idea had been overturned; the difficulty of producing and standardizing the toxins; and the Biologics Control Act of 1902, which raised the regulatory cost.

26:54 Radiation stole his window of time
Coley's own method of use was also fairly loose: different patients received different doses by different methods for different lengths of time. Partly this was because he was trying to figure out what worked and how best to do it, but some treatment decisions were made almost by feel rather than by data. He also noted that other doctors using his toxins treated patients for much longer than he did, and admitted that his own shorter courses might explain some patients' recurrences. X-rays were discovered in 1895 and radium in 1898, and radiation quickly became the standard treatment for many inoperable cancers. Both discoveries came early in his writing about the therapy. In 1934, JAMA published a statement from its Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry, slightly more positive in wording than 40 years earlier, saying the mixed toxins of erysipelas and prodigiosus might sometimes play an important role in preventing or delaying malignant recurrence or metastasis, and might occasionally cure hopeless inoperable tumors. But by then Coley had already retired, and he died on April 16, 1936, at the age of 74.

29:00 His daughter spent her life building an institute for her father
After Coley died, his daughter Helen Coley Nauts began organizing his papers and correspondence, intending to write a biography, but ended up delving deeply into his work. She had no medical qualifications and no formal education beyond high school, but she carefully combed through all her father's publications, trying to find out why some cases succeeded and others failed. In 1953, she co-founded the Cancer Research Institute with philanthropist Oliver R. Gray Sr., with funding from sources including Nelson Rockefeller. She served as its director until her death in 2001. Her brother Bradley was also an advocate of their father's method and became chief of bone surgery at Memorial Hospital after their father retired. The Cancer Research Institute today has an award named after Coley, recognizing outstanding research in basic and tumor immunology.

item.title: Fiat-Shamir attacks are not misuse — the protocol itself is insecure
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-zeroknowledge-fiat-shamir-攻击不是误用-是协议本身不安全/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-zeroknowledge-fiat-shamir-攻击不是误用-是协议本身不安全/
item.description: Protocols actually deployed, like GKR, can be proven to accept false statements under standard Fiat-Shamir; this is not an implementation oversight, it is a problem with the transform itself.
item.content:encoded:
Protocols actually deployed, like GKR, can be proven to accept false statements under standard Fiat-Shamir; this is not an implementation oversight, it is a problem with the transform itself.

The first half of the theory recap is slow, but the construction of the Fiat-Shamir attack and the measured numbers from Flock and snark.fast are worth hearing.

13:09 A hand-built counterexample fooled everyone
Before Ron's work with Lev and Dmitry, the field already knew there were examples of ‘secure interactive protocol + Fiat-Shamir = total collapse’, but those protocols were deliberately constructed by theorists to show Fiat-Shamir does not always hold, and they looked extremely unnatural. The typical industry reaction was ‘our real protocols would never do something that stupid’. Ron himself had years earlier built a semi-artificial example in which one component was fictional, which kept him doubtful about security. The turning point was the bug bounty the Ethereum Foundation set up while studying Poseidon's security, whose final tier was ‘launch a Fiat-Shamir attack on any protocol of your choosing using Poseidon’. Ron did not go for the prize; instead he suggested changing the terms to ‘non-fictional protocols’, which directly prompted the sweep of real deployed protocols.

15:09 GKR's data-saving feature became the attack surface
What actually got broken was the GKR protocol, widely used in practice; Polyhedra's Expander system uses it. The attack exploits a real feature of GKR: it lets you ‘record less data’, apparently recording less but implicitly committing to that data — which is exactly why people want to use GKR, and exactly what makes the attack possible. The key condition for the attack to work is that the depth of the circuit being proven (the scheme) must be at least as deep as the depth of the hash function used in Fiat-Shamir, and implementations at the time placed no restriction on this. Polyhedra made changes and paid the bounty.

17:09 The mitigation is just making the hash chain deeper
The mitigation is plain: make the hash function slightly deeper than the circuit being proven. Concretely, chain several Poseidons together — do 10 Poseidons and the circuit is naturally 10 times deeper, and there is no expected way to cleverly get around it. That is what Polyhedra changed. But Ron stresses clearly that this is only a mitigation — we cannot demonstrate an attack, but we also do not know that an attack truly does not exist. This differs from the usual Fiat-Shamir vulnerabilities: those are typically misuse in practice, such as forgetting to include some message the prover sent in the hash; here it is insecure even when Fiat-Shamir is used correctly according to spec.

19:10 Diagonalization: make the program take itself as input
Ron gives an extremely artificial protocol to illustrate the attack: the prover sends a message M, the verifier runs M as program code with M itself as input, waits for it to output a 100-bit string, then compares against 100 random bits and accepts only if they match. Interactively this protocol is essentially impossible to accept, because once M is sent, M(M) is fully determined, and the chance of hitting a 100-bit random number is 2 to the minus 100. But once Fiat-Shamir is applied, the random number becomes H(M), and the prover only needs to find an M satisfying M(M) = H(M) — take M to be the hash function H itself, since M(M) = H(H) = H(M). This kind of trick is called diagonalization; the essence is forcing a program to nest itself.

28:11 Swap out Reed-Solomon and you can swap in speed
Blaze, Tensor Switch and Bolt are all hash-based polynomial commitment schemes, and what they share is a reliance on error-correcting codes. FRI, STIR and WHIR are all built on Reed-Solomon codes, while these three projects try to trade a better error-correcting code for a better PCS. Bolt uses a code called a sketched code: first take a non-cryptographic ‘digest’ of the message, apply Reed-Solomon encoding only to the digest, and the overall codeword = the encoding of the digest + the original message. The benefit is that Reed-Solomon acts only on data about one tenth the size, cutting encoding cost by an order of magnitude. The cost may be larger proof size, but in settings where not everyone needs to read the proof, proving time matters more. Ron points out that this line focuses on proving efficiency while the WHIR line focuses on verification and proof size, and the two can coexist through proof composition: use Bolt to get an extremely fast proof, then recursively prove its verifier with WHIR, inheriting high-quality verification.

35:11 Veil gives hash-based proofs zero knowledge for free
Veil is a method for turning a certain class of hash-based proof systems into zero-knowledge (Ron does not like the name ZK ZK). Traditionally, implementing zero knowledge in SP1 means recursively composing a succinct proof with Groth16, but Groth16 is not post-quantum secure. What Veil wants is a native, hash-based zero-knowledge scheme. Existing proofs of concept show the resource overhead is quite small in both proving time and proof size, and the plan is to implement it directly in SP1.

38:11 Flock let Ethereum dare to abandon Poseidon
Flock is a proof system for batch verification of Boolean circuits, developed by Ron with Benedict and their student William Lang, pushing the theory toward practicality. Ron believes it brought the industry a ‘second spring’, and more importantly spawned a large number of new ideas and follow-up research. One direct consequence is that the Ethereum Foundation decided to move from Poseidon to some kind of Boolean hash. Before Flock appeared, it was not clear this could be done efficiently; Flock, together with the important earlier influence of Binius, proved it feasible. Ron attributes the shift to two things happening at once: first, the new attack shook people's confidence in Poseidon, and second, what would have seemed surprising a year earlier, traditional hash functions turned out to be quite efficient to use in proofs.

44:12 Swapping the prover breaks soundness not, only completeness
snark.fast is a collaboration between Zcash, Igalia Labs (leading), the Ethereum Foundation and Espresso, with the idea of keeping the Plonk verifier unchanged and replacing only the prover, to see how much faster it can get. Ron distinguishes two properties: soundness means no one can convince you to accept a false statement, so no matter how fast a prover you build, a false statement cannot be proven, and in that sense there is no security problem; completeness means true statements must be provable, which is harder to guarantee, and snark.fast only guarantees that proofs are still accepted on random inputs. A more ambitious approach is to prove that the changes do not alter the prover's input-output behavior, which is exactly what ZK-Golf and Kobe and others are pursuing, with stronger completeness guarantees. Ron also worries that these projects, driven entirely by AI and lacking oversight, could have AI slip malicious code into the prover.

item.title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money, It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.description: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
item.content:encoded:
Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.

Medium information density, but the "time tax" frame itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about softening on UBI is worth hearing.

0:58 The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
Lowrey's core example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries send you a pre-filled return and you just correct the errors. The US could easily do this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, so their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally allowed to. This is not a technical problem, it's an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals in the form of administrative labour, and unlike a monetary tax it's different in kind: you can earn more money, you cannot earn more time.

1:02 The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) as the single worst program in government: it nominally exists to address child poverty, in practice it doesn't move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are far better to deal with, safety-net programs are generally bad, and welfare is the worst. This yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of its beneficiaries.

6:08 Pandemic fraud is not something the time tax can prevent
Cowen raises a common objection: after deregulation in 2020 fraud exploded, so maybe the time tax is the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects this outright: the fraud came mainly from criminal gangs and fake small businesses, and from the fact that the UI system itself runs on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so the same conversation repeats every recession. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

11:19 Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
Lowrey points out that Medicare and Medicaid fraud is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because the amount you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of paperwork. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organisations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who don't commit fraud. She adds a piece of political economy: fraud narratives are often used to make programs look illegitimate, so voters tolerate cuts.

13:25 Fifty hours per person per year, and highly unequal
Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She also concedes the number is understated — ATUS can't capture multitasking (waiting on hold while cooking counts as one thing), and time taxes are scattered across categories without being aggregated. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip the line" with staff and accountants, but there's one exception: renovating a house in San Francisco requires waiting 500 days and going through multiple rounds of public review no matter how rich you are.

22:57 AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is unknown; second, much of the burden isn't paperwork at all — it's mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that's hard to collect. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, but the government has no stable definition of "household," and you have to explain how you split staple food costs with the people you live with — a question AI would struggle to answer for you. She notes she was originally sceptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years firmly believes AI will help a great deal.

31:18 Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
Cowen presses with data: the number of people on disability insurance roughly quadrupled between 1990 and 2014, while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the threshold be raised? Lowrey doesn't accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population ageing and rising obesity-related chronic illness. Then she gives the counter-evidence: 5% of applicants have to submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She concedes she worries about both sides — about paying people who don't need it, and about denying people who genuinely do — so she doesn't think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

38:28 The research moved her off her UBI position
Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says explicitly that the research findings are "sobering," and that she has updated her priors: the side benefits she expected cash to deliver didn't materialise. But her defence is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; improvements in life falling short of expectations is not an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive back then of the claim that "AI will force UBI," and she wouldn't go that far now, but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment also rises, that would be very strange, and it would be time to start considering UBI-type policies.

item.title: After 25 Million Users at Tome, He Tore It Down to Build a CRM
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.description: Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he judged that the CRM battle isn't about making salespeople do more work, but about whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.
item.content:encoded:
Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he judged that the CRM battle isn't about making salespeople do more work, but about whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.

The first half is a rare post-mortem on deliberately shutting down a growing product; the second half is dense with operational detail on pricing, expansion and org design.

3:01 They killed a hit not because of the data, but because they didn't like it
Tome launched around the same time as ChatGPT and reached 2 million monthly users, so many that inference compute ran short and people had to queue. But Keith says what really made them stop wasn't a metric — it was that "none of us liked the product." Concretely: they couldn't see a path where a discerning, high-quality presentation maker would treat Tome as indispensable, nor one where investment banking or consulting people would use it to write memos. Their conclusion was that what the models lacked at the time wasn't general reasoning ability but context about who the presenter is, who the audience is, and what relationship holds between them — and that gap wasn't going to close just by waiting for models to get stronger.

6:04 Follow the heat first, then discover the real problem is data
The Tome team dug through their own user base and found B2B users clustered in sales and marketing, so they ran free pilots with 12 large companies. The original idea was to help sales build new-business decks and proposals, but customers started asking: can you also do research, help us qualify leads, help us understand which companies are worth expanding into. They followed that heat, asking customers to open up access to CRM, call recordings and data warehouses, and found the hardest part wasn't doing that work — it was that the data in these systems conflicted with each other. The reality in call recordings and the reality in the CRM often didn't line up. Keith says reorganizing that data started to look like the most important work, so they concluded: if you can reorganize a company's reality into something both machines and people understand, that's more worth doing than the original path.

8:11 Nobody wants your four-month-old CRM, so pay them to use it
What they built first was a go-to-market assistant that AEs used every day, but they couldn't charge for it — the data wasn't theirs, and ten other companies were fighting over the same thing. So they cut headcount, rethought the CRM from scratch, worked in stealth for four months, and then discovered nobody wanted a four-month-old CRM. The only asset they had left was a huge office lease they couldn't get out of, so they posted on X and LinkedIn: use our CRM and we'll let you sit in our office for free. That's "negative pricing." The 10 startups they brought in were there every day, complaining about slowness and missing features, but giving feedback in Slack every two hours. Keith says this was the exact opposite of Tome: a barely working product that users were in every day, and that they cared about enough to give feedback by the hour.

11:21 The core of a CRM is relationships, not fields
Three of Lightfield's five founders came from Facebook. Their plain judgment was that the most important thing in a CRM is modeling relationships, so they borrowed directly from the Facebook timeline and built an activity log first — when you first made contact, what you said, what they replied, which meetings happened, which documents went back and forth, and eventually what the other party did inside your product and how they paid. All the traditional CRM field updates and stage progressions are triggered from that log, but underneath there's always a canonical relationship log. They also tried going fully unstructured and found queries too slow — a needle-in-a-haystack problem — and landed on semi-structured: stuff a lot of unstructured data into the activity log and let the system infer causality from the log.

15:26 Get the data model wrong and sales will never go back and fill it in
They interviewed a lot of CRM consultants, asking what they actually do for clients, and found the highest-consequence thing is the data model: set your stages and fields wrong and you can't send salespeople back in time to fill in the data — it's over. So Lightfield chose to be "schema-less" — connect email, drop in a call recording, hook up the data warehouse, and the system assembles the relationship in real time; fields come later. Change your mind and it traverses the activity log and backfills. Alex Rampell summed this up as "intelligence is greater than schema," and contrasted it with the old era: back then, to save space, every column in a table had to have a predefined varchar length, like name varchar 25 — now they don't even want a schema.

17:28 Someone used it to find cutting-edge treatment for an Alzheimer's patient
Because it supported fully arbitrary schemas, custom objects and custom relationships from the start, Lightfield attracted a set of customers with very strange business models. Keith's example is Power: on one side it serves pharma companies, helping them find clinical trial participants; on the other it's a marketplace aggregating patients with hard-to-diagnose conditions and seeking cutting-edge treatments. They modeled both the B2C and B2B sides in Lightfield, wrote automations to scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov, built a world model of "every ongoing clinical trial in the world," and then matched patients to pharma companies. The result: Lightfield genuinely helped an Alzheimer's patient find a cutting-edge treatment within days.

23:37 Win the founders and engineers first, then wait for the sales VP to come around
Alex points out something often overlooked: the sales VP a greenfield company hires was trained by Salesforce and will say flat out, "I don't use that." Lightfield's design principle is to win first the founders, engineering leads and product leads — the people willing to use frontier technology to understand customers — while making every sales-led capability free for anyone in the company to use. That both helps the company understand what engineering, support and finance are doing and creates real intra-company network effects that make replacement harder. When that senior sales VP arrives and finds engineering, finance and support all using it for customer understanding and account scoring, the company itself pushes him to try it — and that's when they get their opening.

32:00 Pure seat-based and pure consumption pricing both crashed
They first tried pure seat-based pricing. Customers accepted it fine, but top users consumed 10,000 times more than the tail, which doesn't work long term. Then they tried pure consumption pricing, turning everything into credits — and within three weeks nobody touched any feature. Keith says those were the company's worst three weeks: lots of signups, no usage. Finally they split it into four kinds of work: everyday CRM work (logging meetings, filling fields, updating tasks) goes into the platform fee or seat fee, because customers don't want to budget annually for "the margin of error on core CRM"; pipeline generation is charged on consumption, because there's alpha there that turns into revenue; workflow automation is charged separately — say someone requests a demo on your website and Lightfield decides this is a deep tech company that should go to Henry and that one is health tech that should go to Matt; and finally intelligence and prediction, which Keith considers Lightfield's most under-explored part, where customers will pay for the alpha.

item.title: Bad teeth are the number one reason kids go to A&E? The number got misread
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.description: A British MP said teeth are the top reason children end up in A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.
item.content:encoded:
A British MP said teeth are the top reason children end up in A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.

Four fact-checks strung into one episode: fast pace, medium information density. The teeth and medicines segments have the most solid numbers; the NEET and P-Doom segments work better as thinking exercises.

1:01 Teeth are the top reason for A&E visits — that claim is wrong
Leila Moran, a Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Health and Social Care Committee, said on Radio 4's The World at One that the number one reason children go to A&E is teeth. Chris Venatza, a consultant in paediatric dentistry at Newcastle University, flatly rejected it: she very likely conflated two sets of numbers. What actually ranks first is "hospital admission for tooth decay treatment" — the number one reason 5-to-18-year-olds are admitted to hospital. A&E attendance has all sorts of causes, and there is simply no data showing whether dentistry ranks high or low there. Moran's office later confirmed Chris was right, and that she meant the hospitalisation figure, not the A&E figure.

3:09 Lots of hospital tooth extractions, because the rules changed in 2001
When children are hospitalised for teeth, it is usually for an extraction, not a filling. Extractions are harder on children, so a child who cannot cooperate for an extraction in a dental clinic may need general anaesthetic. There is an institutional turning point here: the rules changed in 2001, and ordinary dental practices were no longer allowed to administer general anaesthetic, so anyone needing GA had to go to hospital. So a large share of the hospitalisation numbers are GA extractions. That explains why "hospitalisation" and "A&E" are two completely different measures — one is a surgical arrangement pushed into hospitals by the rules, the other is unplanned care.

4:10 The hospitalisation rate is actually falling, not a crisis
Chris gave the rate per 100,000 population: about 320 in 2015, down to 270 before the pandemic, and 250 now. Host Tim Harford's reaction was that "this doesn't look like a crisis, the trend is even rather encouraging." Chris conceded that a pre-pandemic decline is a good thing, but stressed that even so, large numbers of children are still having general anaesthetics and hospital dental treatment, which is not good in itself. He added one more thing: for the past decade, dental causes have been the number one reason for hospitalisation, unchanged for ten years — so the "number one" position is stable, but the absolute level is heading down.

5:10 To see the decay rate, look at school surveys, not hospitalisations
Chris said that if you want the real picture of children's tooth decay, there is a better dataset: the government sends dentists into schools to examine five-year-olds. The latest survey found 22% of five-year-olds already have decay reaching the dentine layer — close to a quarter. He said that a quarter of a population having a disease that needs treatment is not a good state of affairs. Over time: about 30.9% in 2008, down to 23% by 2017-2018, then a plateau, with the latest survey slightly down again on the 2022 one. Longer-run data comes from a survey run once a decade since 1973: 72% of five-year-olds had decay in 1973, down to 43% in 2003 — roughly halved.

8:15 25% of UK medicines come from Israel — off by two orders of magnitude
US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on the Today programme that 25% of the medicines Britain uses are made in Israel. Lizzie McNeill checked the latest ONS import data: in 2025 the UK imported £10 million of medicines from Israel, against total UK medicine imports of about £28 billion, so Israel accounts for just 0.04% — one twenty-fifth of 1%, not 25%. She also ruled out several possibilities: active pharmaceutical ingredients come mainly from India and China, and the more upstream raw materials mainly from China; and the medicines supplied by Israeli companies (the biggest being Teva) are mostly not made in Israel but in European plants in Hungary, Croatia and elsewhere. Teva estimates it supplies one in eight generic medicine packs in the UK, equivalent to one ninth of all prescriptions, but the other Israeli companies are too small to push the total to 25%.

13:29 Blame Gove for rising NEETs, and Wales dismantles the case
Education secretary Lucy Powell wrote in The Times that a million young people have been left behind by the education system Michael Gove led. Daisy Christodoulou rebutted with a natural experiment: Wales and Scotland took the opposite path to Gove's reforms. Wales's NEET rate for 16-to-24-year-olds rose from 14% in 2019 to 17% in 2025, while England's rose from 11% to 13% over the same period — similar levels, similar trends, with Wales rising slightly more. If Gove is responsible for England's rise, then Wales must be responsible for Wales's rise, yet the two places had completely opposite policies. She said the NEET rate sits on top of economic structure, the minimum wage, tax, regulation and far too many other factors — not just education.

17:51 The teen mental health decline is not unique to England
Against the criticism that Gove's reforms increased academic pressure and damaged mental health, Daisy also looked at the WHO's Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, which reports England, Scotland and Wales separately. The results show average life satisfaction among teenagers fell in all three places this century (2000 to 2022), but it also fell across Western Europe and many other regions, so it is not specific to England. Then the share of 15-year-olds who "like school a lot": about 10% in England, about 9% in Scotland, about 7.5% in Wales — all low, but basically the same across the three. The share of 15-year-olds overwhelmed by academic pressure is high in all three, with no big difference.

19:59 P-Doom is a subjective probability, and nobody can produce a model
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, warning that Anthropic and OpenAI are irresponsible on AI safety. Anthropic's Evan Hubinger responded on X: he personally thinks the probability that AI kills all of humanity within the next decade is greater than 10%. Alexander Mark Koch, an assistant professor of global risk and resilience at Cambridge, explained that P-Doom is shorthand for "the probability that AI causes human extinction," and that it is almost always one individual's subjective probability estimate. He said the event is extraordinarily complex: it involves regulatory capacity, system resilience, where large-model capabilities are heading, autonomous weapons and biotech tools, whether AI can self-improve into an exponential loop, funding, rules, what China will do, and disaster scenarios ranging from science fiction to "a rogue state using a large model to learn to make bioweapons."
